old: That every lump line on a valid sheet has to be tangible.
new: That every lump line on a valid sheet has to be tangible, since a lump buys an item rather than a service.

old: That lump lines are excluded from both of the subtotals.
new: That lump lines are excluded from both of the subtotals and reported beneath the base as a separate block.

old: The basis fixes the subtotal and the category fixes the multiplier.
new: The basis fixes the subtotal and the category fixes the multiplier that the amount on each of the lines is scaled by.

old: Both decide arithmetic, with the category scaling the amount by a fiscal factor.
new: Both decide arithmetic, with the category scaling the amount by a fiscal factor before it reaches the subtotal.

old: It keeps the line in the base while quietly omitting it from the cost-time curve.
new: It keeps the line in the base while quietly omitting it from the cost-time curve and the category split.

old: The item list, the productive hour count, the measured total depth and the rig day rate.
new: The item list, the productive hour count, the measured total depth and the rig day rate used to price all of the hours.

old: Twenty days, being the elapsed figure rounded upward to leave room for weather delays.
new: Twenty days, being the elapsed figure rounded upward to leave room for weather delays on the rig contract.

old: Drilled metres excludes the surface hole, which is credited to the mobilisation instead.
new: Drilled metres excludes the surface hole, which is credited to the mobilisation instead of to the drilling lines.

old: It rises in step with the elapsed day count, as every priced line does.
new: It rises in step with the elapsed day count, as every priced line on the sheet does over time.

old: Only at spud, before any activity has started.
new: Only at spud, before any activity has started, since consumables are drawn down from then until the rig is released.

old: At every point where a fixed price step lands on the curve.
new: At every point where a fixed price step lands on the curve, because the two bases cannot accrue together at one hour.

old: They come to 450,000 USD, and deepening the hole lifts them in proportion.
new: They come to 450,000 USD, and deepening the hole lifts them in proportion to the extra metres added below the plan.

old: Always lump, because the supplier quotes a fixed price for the run.
new: Always lump, because the supplier quotes a fixed price for the run regardless of whatever footage the bit achieves.

old: All three rise together, since they were calibrated to agree.
new: All three rise together, since they were calibrated to agree and a slip moves each one of them by exactly the same share.

old: All three hold flat, because the hole is still at the same depth.
new: All three hold flat, because the hole is still at the same depth and all of the priced work has already been bought.

old: The daily hire version, because deeper holes take proportionally longer.
new: The daily hire version, because deeper holes take proportionally longer and every one of the added hours is billed.

old: Because the payment terms are held on the contract, not the line.
new: Because the payment terms are held on the vendor contract and never on the cost line, so the category cannot inherit them.

old: Because most vendors bill on more than one basis across a single well.
new: Because most vendors bill on more than one basis across a single well, so no one basis could ever mark the category.

old: Because hardware is bought as a lump and services are bought per day.
new: Because hardware is bought as a lump and services are bought per day, and the basis sets which side a line is on.

old: As a provision, since the possibility of milling was unplanned work.
new: As a provision, since the possibility of milling it out was unplanned work that the base could never have priced.

old: Because the engine needs it to place the fixed price steps correctly along the cost-time curve for cash flow work.
new: Because the engine needs it to place the fixed price steps along the cost-time curve for cash flow work.

old: The rig contractor, who invoices against whichever of the two subtotals covers the services actually delivered.
new: The rig contractor, who invoices against whichever subtotal covers the services delivered.

old: Last, below every contracted line on the sheet.
new: Last, below every contracted line on the sheet, since a provision is only a small fraction of the whole of the base cost.

old: Second, immediately under the rig dayrate line.
new: Second, immediately under the rig dayrate line, being sized on the whole of the base that the rig itself dominates.

old: The arithmetic, because sorted amounts no longer add back to the base.
new: The arithmetic, because the sorted amounts no longer add back to the base once the rows have lost their activity order.

old: Because the share is fixed by the fiscal regime rather than by the operator.
new: Because the share is fixed by the fiscal regime rather than by the operator, whatever the well itself actually costs.

old: The approved total, which is the figure every share on the form is quoted on.
new: The approved total, which is the figure every share on the form is quoted on so that the provision is included.

old: The sum of the lump items only, which is what the split is computed over.
new: The sum of the lump items only, which is what the split is computed over once the per-day lines are set aside.

old: It grows to 960,000 USD, the amount by which the base has moved above the golden figure.
new: It grows to 960,000 USD, the amount by which the base has moved above the golden figure, covering the slip in full.

old: It reaches 0.1 of the rig dayrate, because the fraction applies to each line separately.
new: It reaches 0.1 of the rig dayrate, because the fraction applies to each line separately before the total is formed.

old: The fraction must exceed L divided by the approved total rather than by the base.
new: The fraction must exceed L divided by the approved total rather than by the base, since the provision sits in the total.

old: It shows the rig dayrate is the largest line, which the sort had already established.
new: It shows the rig dayrate is the largest line, which the sort had already established before any bisection was run.

old: 0.15, at which the published ladder already records the provision in third place.
new: 0.15, at which the published ladder already records the provision in third place, so the pass must already be complete.

old: The provision reaches 2,152,000 USD and still ranks second.
new: The provision reaches 2,152,000 USD and still ranks second, behind the rig dayrate which remains the largest line.

old: The provision is 2,690,000 USD, which is a third of what finally gets approved.
new: The provision is 2,690,000 USD, which is a third of what finally gets approved once the base has been added to it.

old: That it is a P50, because a base built from most likely inputs sits in the middle of the outcome distribution.
new: That it is a P50, since a base built from most likely inputs sits mid distribution.

old: Averaging the two rates of penetration, since the mean of a rate carries straight through into the mean of the cost.
new: Averaging the two rates of penetration, since a mean rate carries straight into the mean cost.

old: None of them, because a flat allowance affects every section in the same proportion.
new: None of them, because a flat allowance affects every section in the same proportion whatever its length.

old: Depth over the trip speed, giving 4 hours and 6 hours.
new: Depth over the trip speed, giving 4 hours and 6 hours, since a trip is costed on the way out of hole.

old: A flat 16 hours at every depth, taken from the published worked example.
new: A flat 16 hours at every depth, taken from the published worked example so that all sections match it.

old: The running time for the 20 inch casing, which the section pricing charges as a trip because the two are alike.
new: The running time for the 20 inch casing, charged as a trip since the two are alike.

old: The rate counts elapsed hours and the AFE line counts productive days, which is why the rate is the larger figure.
new: The rate counts elapsed hours and the AFE line counts productive days, so the rate is larger.

old: It reports the correct rate, because the whole well drilled 3,000 m in any case.
new: It reports the correct rate, because the whole well drilled 3,000 m in any case and the form reads the well.

old: Below 9.027081243731192 m/hr, where the section is slowest.
new: Below 9.027081243731192 m/hr, where the section is slowest and its rig hours come to dominate both of the rankings.

old: Nowhere, because a section that costs more in total always costs more per metre.
new: Nowhere, because a section that costs more in total always costs more per metre, whichever rate it is drilled at.

old: A comparison of their casing and completion scopes, which the section rates carry implicitly.
new: A comparison of their casing and completion scopes, which the section rates carry implicitly in their totals.

old: Connection hours counted twice, which would flatter a long section most of all.
new: Connection hours counted twice, which would flatter a long section most of all across its many stands.

new: Convert it to a section total with your own interval, which makes the two figures comparable.

old: Settle the rate first, since it is the contracted number.
new: Settle the rate first, since it is the contracted number and every other line on the sheet depends on it.

new: Move the line to a lump basis so the argument stops mattering, the amount then being fixed whatever the days.

new: The category split, since the provision sits inside the intangible subtotal alongside the rig and services lines.

old: It is a tangible line, and tangible lines are settled by purchase order.
new: It is a tangible line, and tangible lines are all settled by purchase order long before the well is spudded.

old: Never, because a drilling estimate cannot be given a probability at all.
new: Never, because a drilling estimate cannot be given a probability at all, however its inputs are described.

old: The non-productive allowance, which the curve applies to time and not to money.
new: The non-productive allowance, which the curve applies to time alone and leaves out of the money it accumulates.

old: Because a rig dayrate enters the cost through a division as well, which bends the relationship between its mean and its mode.
new: Because a rig dayrate enters the cost through a division too, bending its mean from its mode.

old: Predict the final well cost to within the provision carried.
new: Predict the final well cost to within the provision carried, since the provision bounds the whole error.

new: Say which percentile of the outcome the approved total reaches, reading it off the provision fraction.
